messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos, a 55-year-old Latin American Navy Officer, has been struggling with the memories of his experience in a war zone. The traumatic event that left such an indelible mark on him occurred several years ago when he was deployed as part of a humanitarian mission to a region ravaged by conflict. During one particularly volatile night, Carlos witnessed the devastating aftermath of a bombing raid that killed dozens of civilians, including children. His sense of helplessness and inability to prevent these losses has haunted him ever since. When Carlos recalls this event, he experiences intense waves of guilt that leave him feeling physically and emotionally drained. The memories are so vivid that they feel as real as the day they happened—a full sensory reliving that transports him back to the scene of devastation. At other times, however, his recall is emotionless; he can recount the details but feels completely numb, as if it had happened to someone else. This oscillation between intense guilt and emotional detachment has become a constant source of internal turmoil. The memory of the event often triggers Carlos’s belief that he is a weak person who failed to protect others. He grapples with the notion that his inaction led to the deaths of innocent civilians, and this guilt weighs heavily on him. Each time he relives the memory, it reinforces these negative beliefs about himself—his weakness and inability to act effectively. Carlos’s relationship has also been affected by these intrusive thoughts and memories. His wife notices his increasing withdrawal and difficulty discussing anything related to his experiences. He often finds himself replaying scenarios in his mind where he imagines intervening more decisively, but the memory of his perceived failure only intensifies his self-blame. This cycle of guilt and reliving the event has created a feedback loop that makes it difficult for him to break free from these thoughts. At work, Carlos’s performance has started to suffer as well. He finds himself distracted by intrusive memories during critical operations, which has led to some missteps in his duties. His commanding officers have noticed a decline in his focus and effectiveness. The pressure at work only serves to exacerbate his negative appraisals, as he feels increasingly inadequate in fulfilling his roles both professionally and personally. What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a particularly distressing episode where the memories overwhelmed him during a meeting with his superiors. He became so consumed by guilt that he had to leave abruptly, feeling humiliated and vulnerable. The incident made him realize that he needed support to manage these overwhelming feelings. Carlos is most afraid of being defined by his perceived failures and continues to struggle with forgiving himself for not doing more during the traumatic event. His hope now lies in finding a way to process these memories without them eroding his sense of self-worth further. He seeks guidance on how to break free from the cycle of guilt and find some measure of peace, both within himself and in his relationships.
